Introduction

Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death worldwide and remains a major public health concern. Lifestyle behaviors like smoking and alcohol use are often discussed as risk factors because they can affect cardiovascular health over time.

Previous research and public health guidance commonly link smoking to higher cardiovascular risk because it can damage blood vessels and increase strain on the heart. Alcohol use is more mixed in research depending on the amount consumed, but heavy or frequent use is often associated with negative cardiovascular outcomes. Because these behaviors are modifiable, they are important to examine when studying heart disease patterns.

The goal of this report is to look at how smoking and alcohol use relate to heart disease status in this dataset. My research question is: How does the percentage of people with heart disease differ between smokers and non-smokers, and between alcohol users and non-users? Understanding these patterns helps communicate how common these behaviors are among people with and without heart disease in the data.

Data and Methods

The data used in this analysis comes from the cardiovascular dataset cardiovascular_diseases_dv3.csv. The dataset contains r nrow(data) observations after import and includes demographic, health, and lifestyle variables.

The key variables used in this analysis are:
	•	CARDIO_DISEASE (0 = no heart disease, 1 = heart disease)
	•	SMOKE (0 = no, 1 = yes)
	•	ALCOHOL (0 = no, 1 = yes)

To answer the research question, I grouped participants by smoking status and alcohol status and compared the distribution of heart disease within each group. I used percent-based visuals (pie charts) to clearly show differences between groups. All code is included so the analysis can be replicated.
library(tidyverse)
library(readr)
library(scales)

data <- read_delim("cardiovascular_diseases_dv3.csv", delim = ";", show_col_types = FALSE)

pink_no <- "salmon"
grey_yes <- "gray40"

data_clean <- data %>%
  mutate(
    heart_disease = factor(CARDIO_DISEASE, levels = c(0, 1),
                           labels = c("No Heart Disease", "Has Heart Disease")),
    smoke_status = factor(SMOKE, levels = c(0, 1),
                          labels = c("No Smoke", "Smoke")),
    alcohol_status = factor(ALCOHOL, levels = c(0, 1),
                            labels = c("No Alcohol", "Alcohol"))
  )
  Results

First, I looked at basic counts to understand how many people in the dataset fall into each category.
data_clean %>% count(heart_disease)

data_clean %>% count(smoke_status) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n), accuracy = 1))

data_clean %>% count(alcohol_status) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n), accuracy = 1))
  Smoking and heart disease

This chart compares smoking status within the “No Heart Disease” group versus the “Has Heart Disease” group.smoke_pie_data <- data_clean %>%
  count(heart_disease, smoke_status) %>%
  group_by(heart_disease) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
         label = percent(pct, accuracy = 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

g_smoke_pie <- ggplot(smoke_pie_data, aes(x = "", y = pct, fill = smoke_status)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  facet_wrap(~ heart_disease) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No Smoke" = pink_no, "Smoke" = grey_yes)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            size = 4.5,
            color = "white",
            fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "How does smoking affect heart disease?", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 16) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 17.5, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12.5, face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

g_smoke_pie
ggsave("pie_smoke_heart_disease_salmon_gray.png", plot = g_smoke_pie,
       width = 8, height = 4.6, dpi = 300, bg = "transparent")
From this chart, we can see whether the share of smokers is noticeably different between the heart disease and no heart disease groups.

Alcohol and heart disease

This chart compares alcohol use within the “No Heart Disease” group versus the “Has Heart Disease” group.
alcohol_pie_data <- data_clean %>%
  count(heart_disease, alcohol_status) %>%
  group_by(heart_disease) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
         label = percent(pct, accuracy = 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

g_alcohol_pie <- ggplot(alcohol_pie_data, aes(x = "", y = pct, fill = alcohol_status)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  facet_wrap(~ heart_disease) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No Alcohol" = pink_no, "Alcohol" = grey_yes)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            size = 4.0,
            color = "white",
            fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "How does alcohol affect heart disease?", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 16) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 17.5, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12.5, face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

g_alcohol_pie
ggsave("pie_alcohol_heart_disease_salmon_gray.png", plot = g_alcohol_pie,
       width = 8, height = 4.6, dpi = 300, bg = "transparent")
This chart shows whether alcohol use appears more or less common among people with heart disease compared to those without.

Discussion

Overall, these results provide an easy way to compare smoking and alcohol use patterns across people with and without heart disease in this dataset. If the “Has Heart Disease” group shows a noticeably higher share of smoking or alcohol use, that suggests these behaviors may be associated with heart disease status in the sample. If the percentages look similar, it suggests smoking or alcohol use may not show a strong difference here.

A major limitation is that this analysis is descriptive and does not control for other factors like age, blood pressure, cholesterol, BMI, glucose, or physical activity. It also cannot prove causation, since the dataset is observational. A stronger follow-up analysis would use a statistical model (like logistic regression) to test whether smoking or alcohol use still matters after controlling for other health variables.
